This message comes from University of Buffalo, where scientists are working to protect the Great Lakes and fresh water supplies around the world from harmful contamination.
Learn more about their research at buffalo.edu/npr.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder. California leaders are pushing back after the Trump administration charged 28 green card holders with fraudulently registering and voting from Member Station KQED, Tyche Hendricks reports.
The charges are part of an escalating campaign, Operation Protect the Vote, to highlight illegal voting by immigrants, which the president says is "rampant."
California Attorney General Rob Bonta says true voter fraud should be punished, but as these arrests show, it's exceedingly rare.
28 out of 23 million registered voters in California is just a drop in the bucket numerically.
The charges come just after federal authorities sued California, over 20,000 registered voters they allege are non-citizens.
A similar challenge in Nevada found zero non-citizens. For NPR News, I'm Tyche Hendricks in San Francisco.
An overnight curfew is in effect in parts of Paris and other parts of the country.
France has been rocked by a wave of violent protests that began as a strike by high school students in a Paris suburb and has ballooned into nationwide protests over schools and the cost of living.
Dominique Moise is a political scientist at the Think Tank Institut Montaigne.
I came into a street that was abandoned to rioters. Police was not there. For the first time in my life, I felt deeply insecure in my own city.
The state had simply disappeared. Security was not around. What I saw were people piling cocktail molotov and other instruments of disorder in my very own street.
Officials say at least 3,000 businesses in France have been ransacked or vandalized.
The Supreme Court announced Monday that it would again take up the issue of race and school admissions, this time focused on several middle schools in Montgomery County, Maryland. NPR Sequoia Carillo reports.
Three years after the Supreme Court struck down affirmative action in college admissions, it will consider the issue of race and admissions for four selective middle schools.
The case focuses on the school's shift to a lottery system that the county says ensures fair admissions opportunities for all students.
A group of parents who sued disagree. They say it discriminates based on race, specifically against Asian-American students.
The case has been dismissed twice by lower courts, but will be argued sometime before the court's term ends next summer. Sequoia Carillo, NPR News.
And you're listening to NPR News.
Australian lawmaker Helen Haynes remains in critical condition after she was hit by a car outside her office.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says the incident was no accident, telling Australian media that it was a deliberate act, and the Home Affairs Minister says the alleged attacker reversed the vehicle and struck Haynes a second time, a 43-year-old man is under arrest.
A new deal announced Monday will keep John Stewart in the Daily Show host chair on Mondays through December 2028.
NPR's Eric Deggans reports on the deal that may help counter fears that the new owners of Skydance will stifle voices critical of Donald Trump.
Hey, welcome to the Daily Show. My name is John Stewart.
Stewart's fans will likely hear that greeting for at least a couple more years, following news the comic will stay on as an executive producer and Monday night host, with the program's correspondence continuing the hosted Daily Show from Tuesday to Thursday.
The Daily Show airs on Comedy Central, which is now part of the larger company Skydance, created by Paramount's purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery.
But though critics have accused Skydance owner David Ellison of currying favour with President Trump, an agreement to extend hosting duties by Stewart, who is a frequent Trump critic, may help push back against that idea.
Eric Deggans, NPR News.
